notes.text: The Mental Health Act 2014 (WA) s 9(2) says: "Any communication with a person under this Act must be in a language, form of communication and terms that the person is likely to understand using any means of communication that is practicable and using an interpreter if necessary and practicable." This is a general duty that applies to every step this referral and examination pathway sets in motion.

The WA Health Language Services Policy (Sept 2011) lists "mental health assessment, diagnosis and treatment" among the health care events that "carry higher risks to consumers and health service providers" where "effective communication is essential", and says that health encounters assessed as high risk "warrant the engagement of interpreters or translators with the highest possible level of competency" (ss 6.4, 6.4.1).

The Mental Health Act 2014 (WA) s 50 says: "To the extent that it is practicable and appropriate to do so, the assessment of a person who is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent must be conducted in collaboration with — (a) Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander mental health workers; and (b) significant members of the person's community, including elders and traditional healers."

The Chief Psychiatrist's Clinical Care Standard: Aboriginal Practice (effective 30 November 2015) lists "Interpreter services (well-resourced and readily accessible)" under its Access criterion, and lists "Traditional Healers" and "Consumer, family, carer and community" under its Governance criterion for partnership in coordinated, culturally capable care.

The Mental Health Act 2014 (WA) s 9(2) says: "Any communication with a person under this Act must be in a language, form of communication and terms that the person is likely to understand using any means of communication that is practicable and using an interpreter if necessary and practicable."

This detention exists to enable a psychiatrist examination. The Mental Health Act 2014 (WA) Schedule 1 (Charter of Mental Health Care Principles) Principle 7 says a mental health service "must provide treatment and care to people of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent that is appropriate to, and consistent with, their cultural and spiritual beliefs and practices and having regard to the views of their families and, to the extent that it is practicable and appropriate to do so, the views of significant members of their communities, including elders and traditional healers, and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander mental health workers."

This form continues detention specifically so a further psychiatrist examination can occur. The Mental Health Act 2014 (WA) s 81 says: "To the extent that it is practicable and appropriate to do so, the examination of a person who is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent must be conducted in collaboration with — (a) Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander mental health workers; and (b) significant members of the person's community, including elders and traditional healers." Section 80(1)(b) also lets the examining psychiatrist have regard to information from "an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander mental health worker" or "a significant member of the person's community, including an elder or traditional healer", though not as the sole basis for the order.
